pageTitle: Cassowary
quote: Each of this powerful bird's 3-toed feet has a dagger-like claw on the inner toe that is up to 4 inches (10 centimeters) long! The cassowary can slice open any predator or potential threat with a single swift kick. ... That long claw also comes in handy when digging for fallen fruit in the leaf litter. ... Cassowaries are frugivores that feed on the fruits of several hundred rainforest plants.
unsupported: "over 4 inches" (the source says up to 4 inches); "if the bird feels cornered"; "shy" and "would much rather vanish into the undergrowth than confront a person"
correctedFact: Each of a cassowary's three-toed feet carries a dagger-like claw on the inner toe up to 4 inches long, and a single swift kick can slice open a predator or other threat. The same claw also helps the bird dig for fallen fruit in the leaf litter of its rainforest home.
note: The page covers all three cassowary species; the claw detail is not limited to the southern cassowary.

pageTitle: Border collie comprehends over 1,000 object names as verbal referents
quote: The authors demonstrated that their dog, Chaser, learned the names of 1,022 objects -- no upper limit is apparent -- they stopped training the dog after three years due to their time constraints, not because the dog could not learn more names. ... The authors admitted that she remembered the names of each of her 1022 toys better than they could. ... Their fourth experiment demonstrated that Chaser could also learn names by exclusion -- inferred the name of a novel object by exclusion of familiar already-named objects.
unsupported: "pick a specific one out of a huge pile just by hearing its name" (the release says she was tested under controlled conditions but does not describe the test setup)
correctedFact: A border collie named Chaser learned the names of 1,022 toys over three years of training, and her researchers stopped only because they ran out of time, not because she hit a limit. She could also work out the name of a new toy by excluding the objects she already knew.
note: Release on Pilley and Reid, Behavioural Processes (2011). The release also notes names learned by exclusion were retained only for short periods.

pageTitle: Pronghorn
quote: Pronghorn are the fastest land animals in North America, reaching speeds up to 55 miles per hour (88 kilometers per hour). This possibly evolved as a way to avoid extinct predators such as the American Cheetah.
unsupported: "the second fastest land animal on Earth after the cheetah" (the source says fastest in North America); "extinct for thousands of years"; "Scientists believe" (the source says possibly)
correctedFact: Pronghorn are the fastest land animals in North America, reaching speeds up to 55 miles per hour. That speed may have evolved to escape predators that no longer exist, such as the American cheetah, so the pronghorn may still be built to outrun a hunter that has vanished.

publisher: NOAA Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary
pageTitle: Invasive Lionfish
quote: Lionfish have 18 venomous spines. Thirteen spines are found at the front of the dorsal fin, two at the front edge of each pelvic fin, and one at the front edge of the anal fin. An encounter with a lionfish can have painful consequences for people and potential predators. ... The first lionfish recorded in the Western Atlantic (east coast of the United States, Caribbean Sea, and Gulf) was a specimen captured near Dania, Florida in 1985. ... The most likely source of these fish was the home aquarium trade. ... By 2009, lionfish were pretty well established along the Atlantic coast and throughout the Caribbean.
unsupported: "rarely fatal to humans"; "one of the most damaging invasive species" (the source says they are the first invasive fish to establish in the Western Atlantic); "preying on more than 70 different reef species" (the source says they eat any fish or invertebrate that fits in their mouths)
correctedFact: Lionfish carry 18 venomous spines: thirteen along the front of the dorsal fin, two on each pelvic fin and one at the front of the anal fin. An encounter with those spines can have painful consequences for people and for any predator that tries to eat one.
extraPoints: Native to the Indo-Pacific, lionfish were first recorded in the Western Atlantic near Dania, Florida, in 1985, most likely from the home aquarium trade, and are now established along the Atlantic coast and throughout the Caribbean
note: NOAA's Ocean Service lionfish page says lionfish consume over 50 species of fish, not 70.

pageTitle: A Mighty Claw: Pinching Force of the Coconut Crab, the Largest Terrestrial Crustacean
quote: The coconut crab, Birgus latro, is the largest terrestrial crustacean ... The maximum force ranged from 29.4 to 1,765.2 N, and showed a strong positive correlation with body mass. Based on the correlation between pinching force and body weight, the force potentially exerted by the largest crab (4 kg weight) reported in a previous study would be 3300 N, which greatly exceeds the pinching force of other crustaceans as well as the bite force of most terrestrial predators.
unsupported: "largest land dwelling arthropod" (the paper says largest terrestrial crustacean); "rivals a lion's bite" (no lion comparison in the paper); "Researchers measured the biggest crabs pinching with over 3,000 newtons" (the highest measured force was about 1,765 N; 3,300 N is an estimate for a 4 kg crab); "easily enough to crack open a coconut shell"
correctedFact: The coconut crab is the largest crustacean living on land, and its claws are extraordinarily strong. Wild crabs on Okinawa pinched with up to about 1,765 newtons, and researchers estimated the biggest known crabs could reach 3,300 newtons, stronger than the bite of most land predators.

pageTitle: シマエナガ：くりくりな目がよく目立つ白い頭
quote: 北海道に分布する亜種、シマエナガだけは顔が真っ白に見える ... エナガのほかの亜種は、目の上から後方にかけて黒色部が縞のように続くが、シマエナガにはそれがない。ただし、幼鳥ではそこがぼやっと黒いので「北海道にシマエナガでないエナガがいた」と見誤られることもある。 ... 冬には「雪の妖精」にも例えられる (Translation: Only the shima enaga, the subspecies found in Hokkaido, looks completely white in the face. Other long-tailed tit subspecies have a black band running back from above the eye; the shima enaga lacks it. Juveniles, however, are faintly dark there. In winter it is likened to a "snow fairy".)
unsupported: "in winter they fluff their feathers for insulation until they look like a round white snowball with a long tail stuck on the back" (the source only says it is likened to a snow fairy in winter)
correctedFact: The shima enaga is the Hokkaido subspecies of the long-tailed tit. Other Japanese long-tailed tits have a black stripe running back from above the eye, but the shima enaga's face is pure white. Juveniles still show a faint dark smudge there, and in winter the birds are likened to snow fairies.
note: Japanese-language page from Canon's corporate bird conservation project. First try, an Ornithological Society of Japan 2004 abstract PDF, could not be read (embedded Japanese fonts).

pageTitle: Spring is for nesting: How birds build nests
quote: The long-tailed tit makes a very comfortable nest that is filled with more than 2,000 feathers, which it gradually removes from the nest as the weather gets warmer during spring. It even coats its nest with lichen and binds it with spider silk, allowing the nest to stretch when full.
unsupported: "shima enaga included" (the page covers the long-tailed tit in general); "enclosed"; "moss"; "instead of the parents needing to rebuild it partway through raising a brood"; "gathered one at a time"
correctedFact: Long-tailed tits build a nest coated with lichen and bound together with spider silk, which lets the nest stretch as it fills up. Inside, it is lined with more than 2,000 feathers, which the birds gradually remove as the weather warms through spring.

pageTitle: エナガ：かわいいシマエナガはエナガの亜種
quote: エナガ Aegithalos caudatus スズメ目エナガ科 全長約13.5cm ... 全長がスズメより小さいうえに、その半分近くを尾羽が占め、体重は10ｇに満たない。 (Translation: Long-tailed tit, total length about 13.5 cm ... Smaller than a sparrow in total length, with close to half of that taken up by the tail feathers, and weighing under 10 g.)
unsupported: "Its name comes from hishaku, a long-handled ladle" (no name origin on this page; the shima enaga page on the same site says "shima" means island, for Hokkaido)
correctedFact: Long-tailed tits, the species the shima enaga belongs to, are tiny: about 13.5 centimeters from beak to tail tip, with close to half of that length made up of tail feathers. They are smaller than a sparrow and weigh less than 10 grams.
note: The measurements are given for the species, which the page title says includes the shima enaga as a subspecies.

publisher: Los Angeles Zoo and Botanical Gardens
pageTitle: Western Gaboon Viper
quote: One of the world's largest and heaviest vipers, the Western Gaboon viper also has the longest fangs of any venomous snake, often measuring two inches long or more and folding up against the roof of the snake's mouth when not in use. ... With the highest venom yield (the amount of venom held in their venom glands at one time) of all venomous snakes, Western Gaboon vipers have a deadly bite
unsupported: "a function of simply being a very large-headed, heavy-bodied snake" (the page does not link yield to body size); "The venom is not the most potent by weight"
correctedFact: The Western Gaboon viper has the longest fangs of any venomous snake, often two inches or more, and they fold up against the roof of the mouth when not in use. It also has the highest venom yield of any venomous snake, meaning the most venom held in its glands at one time.
note: Page is for the Western Gaboon viper (Bitis rhinoceros).

publisher: Los Angeles Zoo and Botanical Gardens
pageTitle: Western Gaboon Viper
quote: As an ambush predator, this nocturnal hunter will lie perfectly still underneath the leaf litter on the forest floor and wait for its prey to pass by. The viper will quickly strike by biting its prey and injecting it with venom. The viper holds onto its victim until it dies, and then consumes the animal whole headfirst.
unsupported: "Most vipers strike, inject and let go, then track the animal down"; "prey is less likely to stagger off somewhere it cannot follow"; "what makes a bite on a person so much worse than the fang length alone suggests"
correctedFact: The Western Gaboon viper is an ambush hunter that lies perfectly still under leaf litter on the forest floor until prey passes. When it strikes, it bites and injects venom, then holds onto its victim until it dies before swallowing it whole, headfirst.
note: The same page says bites on people are rare and partly attributes the low number of deaths to the snake's calm, slow-moving nature.

publisher: Journal of the Royal Society Interface (2013)
pageTitle: Snakes mimic earthworms: propulsion using rectilinear travelling waves
quote: In rectilinear locomotion, snakes propel themselves using unidirectional travelling waves of muscular contraction, in a style similar to earthworms. In this combined experimental and theoretical study, we film rectilinear locomotion of three species of snakes, including red-tailed boa constrictors, Dumeril's boas and Gaboon vipers. ... The body trajectory for rectilinear locomotion is linear, which minimizes the path length travelled by parts of the body and, in turn, the sounds produced. Thus, rectilinear locomotion is naturally applied to stealthy activities such as stalking prey. ... Rectilinear locomotion is a slow mode of locomotion
unsupported: "heavy enough that the side-to-side motion most snakes use works badly for it" (the paper does not give weight as the reason); "closer to a caterpillar" (the paper compares it to earthworms)
correctedFact: Gaboon vipers can travel in a straight line instead of slithering side to side, pushing forward with waves of muscle contraction along the belly, much as an earthworm does. The gait is slow, and because the body follows a straight path it makes less noise, which suits stalking prey.
note: Text read from the authors' PDF hosted by Georgia Tech (hoogle.gatech.edu); the URL given is the journal DOI.

pageTitle: Kākāpō
quote: The kākāpō is a large, green, flightless parrot with an owl-like face and a waddling gait. It is nocturnal, the world's only lek-breeding parrot, and possibly the longest-lived bird species, living 60–90 years. It is also the heaviest parrot species, with males weighing up to 4 kg.
unsupported: "the world's only flightless parrot" (the source says flightless, not the only one); "unusual among parrots"; "a deep booming call that can carry for miles"; "individuals recorded living past 80 years" (the source gives a possible lifespan of 60 to 90 years)
correctedFact: The kakapo is a nocturnal, flightless parrot from New Zealand and the heaviest parrot species in the world, with males weighing up to 4 kg. It may also be the longest-lived bird species, with an estimated lifespan of 60 to 90 years.
extraPoints: Males make a deep booming call during the mating season
Kakapo may be the longest-lived bird species

pageTitle: Maine Coon Cat
quote: the largest of all pedigreed cats, the Maine Coon Cat is quite appropriately known as the gentle giant of the cat fancy. ... This is a slow-maturing breed that can take up to three years to reach full growth. While it is not unusual for a mature male's weight to reach or exceed 20 pounds, females are usually smaller.
unsupported: "males often weighing 15 to 25 pounds" (the source says a mature male often reaches or exceeds 20 pounds); "measuring 40-plus inches from nose to tail"; "The longest Maine Coon on record, a cat named Stewie, measured 48.5 inches"
correctedFact: The Maine Coon is the largest of all pedigreed cats, known as the gentle giant of the cat fancy. It is also a slow-maturing breed that can take up to three years to reach full growth, and mature males often reach or exceed 20 pounds.
extraPoints: The longest Maine Coon on record, Stewie, measured 48.5 inches

pageTitle: Okapi
quote: With striking white-and-black striped legs, an okapi ... looks like it could be related to a zebra. ... Okapis are indeed the only close living relative of giraffes. ... An okapi's stripes ... offer great camouflage when an okapi stands in the partial sunlight filtering through the dense rainforest. ... Okapis live in tropical rainforests in the northeast region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo ... An okapi's dark tongue is long enough to reach its eyes and ears.
unsupported: "14 to 18 inches long" (the source gives no length); "lick its own eyes and ears clean" (the source says reach)
correctedFact: The okapi looks like it could be related to a zebra, thanks to its striped legs, but it is the only close living relative of the giraffe. Like a giraffe, it has a long, dark, prehensile tongue, and that tongue is long enough to reach its own eyes and ears.
extraPoints: Okapis live only in the rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where their stripes work as camouflage in dappled light

pageTitle: Movement and storage of nematocysts across development in the nudibranch Berghia stephanieae (Valdés, 2005)
quote: One form of defensive sequestration involves animals that sequester stinging organelles (nematocysts) from their cnidarian prey. While it has been hypothesized that nematocysts are identified by specialized phagocytic cells for internalization and storage, little is known about the cellular and developmental mechanisms of this process in any metazoan lineage. ... Like other nudibranchs, B. stephanieae sequesters nematocysts in a structure called the cnidosac that is found at the tips of finger-like dorsal projections called cerata.
unsupported: "jellyfish" (the paper says cnidarian prey; its study species eats sea anemones); "Scientists are still working out exactly how it keeps the stolen stingers from firing along the way" (the open question in the paper is how the stingers are selected and stored)
correctedFact: Some nudibranchs eat stinging cnidarians such as sea anemones and keep the prey's stinging capsules instead of digesting them. The capsules move from the gut into a sac at the tips of finger-like projections on the slug's back called cerata, where they are stored for defense. How the slug selects and stores them is still poorly understood.

pageTitle: Gila monster: meet the lizard whose venomous bite is saving lives
quote: The desert-dwelling Gila monster (Heloderma suspectum) is the United States' largest and only native venomous lizard. ... A breakthrough discovery found that a hormone in the lizard's saliva, exendin-4, could be used to treat type 2 diabetes. Exendin-4 is in many ways similar to the human hormone GLP-1 ... Exenatide is a synthetic version of exendin-4, sold under the commercial names Byetta and Bydureon.
unsupported: "its slow metabolism lets it get by on just a few meals a year, living off fat stored in its tail"; "later helped inspire the GLP-1 medications behind Ozempic"
correctedFact: The Gila monster is the largest and only native venomous lizard in the United States. A hormone in its saliva, exendin-4, resembles the human hormone GLP-1, and a synthetic version called exenatide became a type 2 diabetes drug sold as Byetta and Bydureon.
extraPoints: A slow metabolism lets the Gila monster survive on a few meals a year, living off fat stored in its tail

pageTitle: Kea
quote: Kea are a clever parrot that only live in New Zealand. They are one of the smartest birds in the world and are famous for solving problems. ... Kea are very curious and love to explore. They often play, investigate things, and figure out how things work. ... Kea live in alpine (mountain) areas and forests and some also live near sea level across the South Island ... The playful behaviour of kea can also lead to damage to cars and buildings.
unsupported: "the world's only alpine parrots"; "can outperform some primates in lab tests"; "stripping rubber from cars and snatching gloves, wallets, and food from tourists at ski resorts" (the source says damage to cars and buildings); "Researchers think this constant tinkering with new objects is how kea learn about their world"
correctedFact: Kea, parrots found only in New Zealand, are among the smartest birds in the world and famous for solving problems. They are very curious, playing with and investigating new things to figure out how they work, and that playful streak can lead to damage to cars and buildings.
note: The source also says kea range from alpine areas down to sea level, so "living high in New Zealand's mountains" is only part of the picture.

pageTitle: Dachshund History: The Badger Dog's Fascinating Past
quote: But its name, which in German translates as "badger dog," tells a completely different story. ... by the 18th Century German foresters and hunters began to breed their type consistently, paving the way for the breed we know today. ... The dogs obviously had to have short legs so they could easily fit in the badger holes.
unsupported: "chondrodysplasia, a form of dwarfism that keeps the leg bones short while the rest of the body grows normally"; "That same long spine is why the breed is prone to disc problems later in life"
correctedFact: Dachshund means badger dog in German, and the breed was built for the job. By the 18th century, German foresters and hunters were breeding the dogs consistently, giving them short legs to fit into badger holes and a bold, independent streak for facing badgers head-on underground.
extraPoints: The short legs come from chondrodysplasia, a form of dwarfism
The long spine makes the breed prone to disc problems
note: First try, the AKC breed page, renders by script and returned no text.

pageTitle: Pygmy Marmoset
quote: it's a pygmy marmoset, the world's smallest monkey! ... A full-grown pygmy marmoset could fit in an adult human's hand, and it weighs about as much as a stick of butter. ... tree sap is their favorite food. They ... gouge a hole in the bark or vine with their sharp lower teeth ... Pygmy marmosets have certain trees they like within their territory; they can make up to 1,300 holes in each tree! ... They can make sounds so high in pitch that humans can't hear them.
unsupported: "letting them coordinate with their group without alerting nearby predators"
correctedFact: Tree sap is the favorite food of the pygmy marmoset, the world's smallest monkey. It gouges holes in bark or vines with its sharp lower teeth using an up-and-down sawing motion, laps up the sap that pools there, and can make up to 1,300 holes in a single favorite tree.
extraPoints: Pygmy marmosets are the smallest monkeys, small enough to fit in a hand and about as heavy as a stick of butter
Some of their calls are too high-pitched for humans to hear

pageTitle: Excessive luminosity fades the skin color of cardinal tetra
quote: Loss of skin color was observed when cardinal tetra was exposed to intense light. The melanic and neon stripes became pale due to a reduction in melanophores densities. On the other hand, the color of the red stripe was intensified due to the proliferation of erythrophores. ... We suggest that in nature, the paleness of the skin may represent a camouflage strategy during the hours of the day with greater luminosity in the black water of the Rio Negro. Fading the skin color can help this species to visually confuse potential predators.
unsupported: "the metallic stripe actually functions as camouflage, reflecting available light in a way that creates false or confusing targets" (the paper suggests the fading of the stripes in bright light may be camouflage, and does not describe reflected light or false targets); "actually" (the paper offers it as a suggestion)
correctedFact: A cardinal tetra's skin color shifts with the light. Under bright light its dark and neon blue stripes pale while the red stripe deepens, and researchers suggest this fading may act as camouflage in the dark blackwater of the Rio Negro during the brightest hours, helping the fish confuse predators.
note: The false-target idea matches a 2009 neon tetra study (Ikeda and Kohshima, mirror-image decoy) rather than anything shown for the cardinal tetra.

pageTitle: Sailfin Molly (Poecilia latipinna) - Species Profile
quote: Native Range: Atlantic and Gulf Coast drainages from Cape Fear drainage, North Carolina, to Veracruz, Mexico. Restricted to coastal areas in most of range ... Ecology: Generally occurs in shallow, slow-moving surface waters of marshes, ponds, streams, ditches, swamps, and estuaries. Commonly associated with vegetation. Widely tolerant of temperature, salinity, and low oxygen levels.
unsupported: "coastal saltwater lagoons" (the source says estuaries); "unusually wide range of salinities for an aquarium fish"; "sometimes just a short distance apart"
correctedFact: The sailfin molly is widely tolerant of salinity, temperature and low oxygen. In its native range along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, from North Carolina to Mexico, it lives in shallow, slow water of marshes, ponds, streams, ditches, swamps and estuaries, mostly near the coast.
note: Source covers the sailfin molly only. First try, the USGS shortfin molly profile, had no salinity text.

pageTitle: Emx2 underlies the development and evolution of marsupial gliding membranes
quote: Patagia are specialized skin membranes that enable animals to glide ... patagia have arisen convergently among diverse mammals, including different species of rodents, bats, colugo and Australian marsupials. ... Together, our results suggest that patagia repeatedly originated through a process of convergent genomic evolution, whereby regulation of Emx2 was altered by distinct cis-regulatory elements in independently evolved species.
unsupported: "glide the exact same way, a furred membrane stretched from wrist to ankle"; "each arriving at a similar structure through a different genetic path" (the paper studied marsupials only, and found separate gliders changed control of the same gene, Emx2)
correctedFact: Gliding membranes have evolved again and again in unrelated mammals, including rodents such as flying squirrels, bats, colugos and Australian marsupials such as the sugar glider. In marsupials, a 2024 study found that separate gliding species reached the trait by altering control of the same gene, Emx2, through different genetic switches.
note: Text read from the open accepted manuscript at par.nsf.gov. The paper does not name flying squirrels specifically, only rodents.

pageTitle: Spawning in Ancistrus (Siluriformes: Loricariidae) with comments on the evolution of snout tentacles as a novel reproductive strategy: larval mimicry
quote: Most species of Ancistrus exhibit a striking sexual dimorphism, mature males having an elaborate complex of enlarged fleshy tentacles on the snouts. Snout tentacles appear to be modifications of the fleshy cutaneous sheath that surrounds the base of an odontode (integumentary tooth) and are best developed in breeding males. The tentacles are thought to serve as accessory sensory structures because they are covered with taste buds. ... In Ancistrus, as in nearly all Ancistrinae, the cheek spines often are more developed in males ... and are used in agonistic displays and combat.
unsupported: "they're odontodes" (the paper says the snout tentacles are fleshy outgrowths of the skin sheath around an odontode, not odontodes themselves); "also found in smaller form on the gill covers of both sexes" (smaller tentacles occur on the snout margin of females and juveniles); "Males use them ... to spar with rival males over a cave" (the paper says the cheek spines, not the tentacles, are used in combat)
correctedFact: The branching bristles on a mature male bristlenose pleco's snout are fleshy tentacles that grow from the skin sheath around tiny tooth-like odontodes, and they are covered with taste buds. Females and juveniles grow smaller, fewer ones. Males also carry larger cheek spines, true odontodes, which they use in displays and fights.
note: Source by Sabaj, Armbruster and Page, hosted on Armbruster's Auburn University page. It contradicts the card's central claim, so the card needs a rewrite rather than a trim.

unsupported: Whole card: cherry shrimp eating their own molt to reclaim calcium, and keepers leaving the molt in the tank
note: Searched for Neocaridina or freshwater shrimp exuviae eating and calcium recovery; found only hobbyist sources and an isopod study (Hyloniscus riparius, PLOS ONE 2013), not shrimp.

pageTitle: Larval performance of three amphidromous shrimp species in the genus Caridina (Decapoda: Caridea: Atyidae) under different temperature and salinity conditions
quote: We examined the effects of temperature and salinity on larval survival, duration, and growth of three amphidromous atyid shrimps, Caridina leucosticta, C. multidentata, and C. typus to infer larval dispersal strategy in the sea. ... C. multidentata larvae exhibited an ability to adapt to the wide range of salinity condition (17–34 ppt) ... C. multidentata larvae may be able to disperse broadly under the high salinity condition of the open sea.
unsupported: "even a small, accidental dose of salt can kill a mature amano shrimp outright" and "would die if you tried to acclimate it into a saltwater tank as an adult" (the card's headline claim; not in the source); "within their first days of life"
correctedFact: Amano shrimp larvae are amphidromous: they hatch in fresh water but develop at sea. In a 2021 rearing study, larvae of this species survived to the juvenile stage across salinities from 17 to 34 ppt, from brackish water to full seawater, suggesting they can disperse widely in the open sea.
note: The larval half is supported; the adult half, which is the card's title, is not. C. multidentata is the amano shrimp.
